rv.q: Edmundson's play may be a history lesson, but it rescues Anne from the shadows and offers a rousing hymn to female agency.
It’s worth seeing for her performance alone but Garai is terrific too, if lacking in redemptive warmth, as the imperious, two-faced power behind the throne.
But this is still an absorbing work that will reward an audience keen for intelligent storytelling.
Helen Edmundson's intelligent and enjoyable history play for the Royal Shakespeare Company
It's a decent, nicely diverse cast... but must things come to a halt quite so often while characters recite the 18th-century equivalent of Wikipedia to each other?
On the downside, this makes the stakes feel lower than they might, especially as Sarah and Anne’s friendship is so strained to begin with.
The pacing lags in places and Hannah Clark’s dark, wood-panelled set serves to further suck the energy out of a play that seems increasingly confused as to what story it wants to tell.
The production proves less gripping than the subject matter.
There should be passion and pain here, though, as well as politics, but we don’t feel it.
Under the direction of Natalie Abrahami, the play also provides an outlet for two superb performances; Emma Cunniffe as Anne and in particular Romola Garai as Sarah Churchill.
The second Act is quite exceptional.

Emma Cunniffe delivers a sympathetic depiction of a troubled monarch trying to save her country and her religion, the goings on around her in Natalie Abrahami’s production but this is hardly another Madness or Wolf Hall.
It's a shame, then, that a tantalizingly ripe slice of distaff history should go so underdeveloped in Helen Edmundson's windy but not especially illuminating play.
Slow, overlong and only intermittently entertaining, Queen Anne feels an awful lot like being back in the classroom – a show you might want to consider playing truant from.
Despite some plodding moments of exposition, it is an enjoyable evening.
A stalwart if stolid history play, elegantly performed.
Queen Anne delivers an intriguing history lesson but never provides the captivating drama that the facts would seem to promise.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this RSC production about a neglected monarch, praising the strong performances by Cunniffe and Garai but finding the play itself static and overly wordy, with a stronger second act.
